questions.question: How do `async` functions and `await` work in JavaScript?
questions.title: How async and await Work
questions.direct_answer: Calling an `async` function always returns a new Promise. Returning a value fulfills it and an uncaught throw rejects it. `await` pauses only that async function until its operand settles, then produces the fulfillment value or throws the rejection reason while other JavaScript work can continue.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the returned Promise, suspension boundary, rejection behavior, and event-loop continuation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying `await` blocks JavaScript globally or that marking a CPU-heavy function `async` moves it to another thread.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe await as suspension and resumption of one function while its outer Promise remains observable by the caller.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Every call to an `async` function returns a Promise, even when the function returns a plain value.
An uncaught exception inside an async function becomes a rejected returned Promise.
`await` unwraps fulfillment and throws a rejection at that expression.
Awaiting a non-Promise still resumes asynchronously with that value.
`await` suspends the current async function, not the entire JavaScript thread.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An `async` function is a function that always returns a new Promise. If its body says `return 42`, the returned Promise fulfills with `42`. If the body throws an error that is not caught, the returned Promise rejects with that error. Returning another Promise makes the outer Promise follow that result.

`await` reads the result of a value or Promise. A fulfilled Promise gives its value to the expression, as in `const user = await loadUser()`. A pending Promise suspends only the current async function. The caller and other JavaScript work can continue, and the function resumes later after the awaited result settles.

The short example shows the order clearly. `load()` prints before its first `await`, then returns a Promise. The caller prints next. After the awaited Promise is ready, `load()` resumes and fulfills its outer Promise. If that awaited Promise rejected instead, the `await` expression would throw inside `load()`, where normal `try` and `catch` could handle it.

`async` and `await` make Promise-based code easier to read, but they do not move work to another thread or make operations parallel. Code before the first `await` still runs synchronously, so a long calculation there blocks the event loop. Use them to express asynchronous dependencies and error flow, and use a worker when CPU-heavy work must run away from the main thread.

`await` reads the result of a value or Promise. A fulfilled Promise gives its value to the expression, as in `const user = await loadUser()`. A pending Promise suspends only the current async function. The caller and other JavaScript work can continue, and the function resumes later after the awaited result settles.

questions.question: When should asynchronous work run sequentially, concurrently with `Promise.all`, or with `Promise.allSettled`?
questions.title: Sequential vs Concurrent Async Work
questions.direct_answer: Await operations sequentially when a later step needs an earlier result. Start independent operations together and await `Promise.all` when every result is required; it preserves input order and rejects on the first observed rejection. Use `Promise.allSettled` when every fulfillment or rejection must be collected.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you distinguish dependency order from concurrency and choose Promise aggregation from failure requirements.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Awaiting independent operations one by one or assuming `Promise.all` cancels unfinished work after a rejection.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention result ordering, fail-fast behavior, all-settled status records, and bounded concurrency for large batches.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Two immediate `await` calls are sequential when the second operation starts after the first finishes.
Call independent async functions before awaiting them, usually inside `Promise.all`.
`Promise.all` fulfills with results in input order, not completion order.
`Promise.all` rejects when one input rejects, but it does not cancel the remaining operations.
`Promise.allSettled` waits for every input and returns a status record for each one.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Run operations sequentially when a later step needs an earlier result. In `const posts = await loadPosts(user.id)`, the posts request cannot start until the user request has produced `user.id`. Authentication before an account request is another real dependency because the second call needs the token returned by the first. Writing two awaits in order is correct here because the dependency, not the syntax, requires that order.

Independent operations should be started before waiting for them. `Promise.all([loadUser(), loadNotices()])` invokes both functions while the array is created, then waits for both results. The result array keeps the original input order even if the notices finish first. One rejection rejects the combined Promise, but it does not cancel the other operation.

Use `Promise.all` when every result is required and one failure should fail the combined operation. Use `Promise.allSettled` when every outcome matters, such as a batch upload that must report both successful and failed files. It waits for all inputs and returns one `fulfilled` or `rejected` record for each input.

Concurrency overlaps waiting time; it does not guarantee parallel CPU execution. Starting thousands of independent requests at once can still overload the browser, network, or server. For a large batch, use a concurrency limit. The choice is therefore: follow real dependencies, select the required failure policy, and then control how much work may run at once.

questions.question: How should errors be handled in an async function, and what happens when `await` is omitted?
questions.title: Async Error Boundaries and Missing await
questions.direct_answer: Use `try` and `catch` around an awaited operation when the current function can handle its rejection. If a Promise is created inside the `try` but neither awaited nor returned through the intended boundary, the block finishes before rejection arrives, so that catch cannot handle it and the work may become an unhandled rejection.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can place rejection handling at the correct async ownership boundary and reason about missing await.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Starting async work inside `try` without awaiting it and expecting the synchronous lifetime of the block to catch later rejection.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish simple Promise forwarding from `return await` inside a local error or cleanup boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Awaited rejection behaves like a throw at the await expression.
Catch only errors the current layer can recover from or translate meaningfully.
A Promise started without `await` can reject after the surrounding `try` has finished.
Return a Promise when the caller should own its completion and failure.
Use `finally` for cleanup such as resetting loading state, not for swallowing errors.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
When an awaited Promise rejects, `await` throws that reason at the same point inside the async function. A surrounding `try` and `catch` can therefore recover, translate the error, or add useful context. If the error is not caught there, the async function finishes by returning a rejected Promise to its caller.

A function should catch an error only when it can make a real decision, such as showing a fallback, translating a low-level error, or resetting local state. For example, a screen can turn a network failure into a visible retry message, while a lower-level helper may not know how the application should recover. Otherwise, returning `saveUser()` lets the caller await and handle that Promise. Logging an error and then returning nothing can accidentally turn a rejection into successful `undefined`.

If `saveUser()` is called inside a `try` without `await`, that block can finish before the Promise rejects, so its `catch` cannot receive the later rejection. The work must be awaited here, returned to a caller, or deliberately detached with its own `.catch(...)`. Losing all three paths creates an unhandled-rejection risk.

Simple forwarding can use `return saveUser()`. Use `return await saveUser()` when a surrounding local `try`, `catch`, or `finally` must observe how that Promise settles before the function leaves the block. `finally` is the right place for outcome-independent cleanup, but it should not silently hide an error that the current layer cannot handle.

If the error is not caught there, the async function finishes by returning a rejected Promise to its caller.

items.label: await
items.detail: Settlement stays inside this function's try, catch, and finally boundary.

items.label: return
items.detail: The caller owns completion and any rejection of the returned Promise.

items.label: detach explicitly
items.detail: Background work attaches its own rejection reporting because nobody awaits it.

beats.spokenText: Simple forwarding can use `return saveUser()`. Use `return await saveUser()` when a surrounding local `try`, `catch`, or `finally` must observe how that Promise settles before the function leaves the block. `finally` is the right place for outcome-independent cleanup, but it should not silently hide an error that the current layer cannot handle.
